nodes.label: Logistics Overhead Ratio
nodes.rationale: (international freight + source handling + last-mile + insurance) ÷ product value, with a viability threshold around 25%. Freight scales with chargeable weight = max(actual, volumetric), so overhead rises with distance and weight and falls with product value.

nodes.label: RULE: Value-Density Beats Proximity
nodes.rationale: A light, expensive item is viable from far away; a heavy, cheap item is uneconomic even from next door. Therefore the business does not 'support routes' — it gates individual orders on economics and picks the route/model that widens the viable zone.

nodes.label: RULE: Minimum Order Value Gate
nodes.rationale: The quote engine reads the minimum-viable-value cell for the order's route and weight and either blocks the order, suggests consolidation, or nudges toward a cheaper pickup point — rather than quoting a price that is mostly shipping.

nodes.label: RULE: Consolidation as a Margin Tool
nodes.rationale: Combining chargeable weight and amortizing handling can cut per-parcel cost by up to ~80%, making it the single biggest lever for moving 'weak' orders into 'viable'. It is therefore a first-class product feature with explicit consolidation windows, not a convenience.

nodes.label: RULE: Category Allowlist by Density
nodes.rationale: Launch categories are high-value, low-weight, low-volume (electronics, cosmetics/fragrance, watches, jewelry, accessories, non-bulky premium fashion); bulky/heavy/low-value goods wait for a heavy-freight lane.

nodes.label: Five-Leg Fulfillment Chain (A–D, points 1–5)
nodes.rationale: Naming legs and handoff points explicitly is what allows each leg to be priced separately, sold separately to merchants, and have its provider swapped independently.

nodes.label: DECISION: Asset-Light (own orchestration, rent metal)
nodes.rationale: Own the orchestration and the data (which point, which leg, which provider, unified tracking) but rent the physical assets — forwarder warehouses, freight carriers, Iranian gig last-mile. Owning warehouses and fleet is a scale-phase decision, never an MVP one.

nodes.label: Model A: Integrated Forwarder + Gig Last-Mile
nodes.rationale: Rated 5/5 for MVP: fastest to launch, asset-light, reuses mature infrastructure on both ends (UAE forwarders, Iranian gig fleets), cleanest compliance profile, and yields the unified tracking data that constitutes the moat.

nodes.label: Model B: PUDO / Pickup-Point Network
nodes.rationale: Out-of-home delivery is roughly 25% cheaper than home delivery and cuts returns cost by up to 60%, so skipping the door last-mile is what turns a bulky low-value order from weak into viable. Added as a phase-2 delivery option using partner shops before any lockers.

nodes.label: Model C: Crowdshipping / Traveler Network
nodes.rationale: Scored 3/5 — a supplementary channel, never the backbone. Capacity is lumpy, liability and authenticity risk are real, and customs exposure (personal-import limits, undeclared goods) is the sharp edge. Confined to Leg B for value-dense items with escrow released on hub scan-in rather than personal handoff.

nodes.label: Model D: Hawala-Style 'Goods Gate' Agent Network
nodes.rationale: Borrows hawala's decoupling of delivery from settlement so a destination agent holding stock can deliver instantly while replenishment flows asynchronously. Scored 2/5 as a general model but 4/5 as a narrow instant-delivery feature for pre-stocked hero SKUs, because the moment agents settle cross-border cash imbalances it becomes an unlicensed informal value-transfer system.

nodes.label: Model E: Own Warehouses + Own Fleet (deferred)
nodes.rationale: Best eventual unit cost and control, but heavy capex and slow to stand up — explicitly deferred to the scale phase and not built for MVP.

nodes.label: RULE: Goods Only, Never Cross-Border Value Transfer
nodes.rationale: Hawala-style value transfer is regulated money transmission and illegal unlicensed. Agents may only ever touch goods, settlement stays inside each jurisdiction, customs are declared properly, personal-import limits are enforced on travelers, and a full audit trail is kept.

nodes.label: Modular 'Sell Legs, Not Bundles' Merchant Toolkit
nodes.rationale: Packages run from full-to-door down to consolidation-only, each separately priced. Merchants who already have local last-mile buy exactly the expensive, hard part (source procurement, international leg, customs) and keep what they are good at — which is also what removes the 'thin middle' commoditization risk.

nodes.label: DECISION: Integrate Iranian Gig Fleets as Leg-D Providers
nodes.rationale: Domestic last-mile in Iran is already solved by AloPeyk, Snapp Box and Miare, so integrating them gives on-demand door delivery with zero capex. The genuinely novel gig layer is the cross-border traveler network, not the domestic one.

nodes.label: BUILD: Last-Mile Provider Abstraction
nodes.rationale: Follows the same pattern as the FX and store-adapter ports so the system can pick AloPeyk vs Snapp Box vs pickup point vs traveler per order on cost, SLA and coverage.

nodes.label: Route Feasibility Matrix (UAE / Turkey / Germany / UK)
DECISION: UAE (Dubai) → Iran Beachhead Lane
nodes.rationale: UAE scores ≈4.1 weighted on freight proximity, forwarder maturity, payment feasibility and customs reliability. Turkey is the strong #2 and lane 2; Germany and the UK justify themselves only as value-dense catalog extensions because rate per kg dominates.

nodes.label: Escrow + Reputation Trust Rails
nodes.rationale: Copied from Grabr and hawala networks: money released only on verified delivery or scan, plus agent/traveler ratings, verification and limits. Built once and reused across travelers, agent gates and pickup points.

nodes.label: AloPeyk / Snapp Box (Iranian gig delivery fleets)
Phase 0.4 Open GATEs (freight quotes, customs, hub partner, last-mile, legal)
